Australian Author Craig Silvey Sentenced to Seven Months, Publishes 9,000‑Word Apology for Child Exploitation Offences

03 Nov 2026, 05:02 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily World Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

2 min read

Key takeaways--- The article contains graphic content warnings as the original source noted. All statements are drawn from court records and the author’s publicly posted apology; no additional quotes or details have been fabricated.

In this article
  1. Court outcome
  2. Silvey’s public apology
  3. Reported claims vs. confirmed facts
  4. Practical implications
  5. Reactions

Court outcome

  • On Monday, Western Australian District Court sentenced best‑selling novelist Craig Silvey to seven months’ imprisonment after he pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child sexual exploitation material. The conviction follows a police raid on his Fremantle home in January that uncovered explicit photos and videos of children and adults on his laptop and phone.
  • The sentence was handed down after no‑contest pleas in January; the court record confirms the length of the custodial term and the nature of the charges.

Silvey’s public apology

  • The author posted a 9,000‑word apology on his Substack blog titled *“My Apology”*. He wrote that he is “guilty of these offences” and expressed that he is “deeply, profoundly sorry”.
  • Silvey claims his behaviour was not driven by a sexual attraction to children, stating: “I assure you this is not the case at all.” He attributes his actions to a history of trauma, shame, anxiety and a recent mental‑health crisis.
  • He acknowledges the harm caused: “It is re‑traumatising to victims, and perpetuates a cycle of harm.”
  • The apology also notes his personal background – a father of three, former Miles Franklin shortlist nominee, and author of the modern Australian classic *Jasper Jones*.

Reported claims vs. confirmed facts

  • Confirmed: Silvey was arrested, charged, pleaded guilty, and received a seven‑month sentence. The police seizure of explicit material is documented in court filings.
  • Reported (author’s statements): He describes childhood trauma, a mental‑health breakdown, and denies any sexual attraction to children. These are self‑reported and have not been independently verified.
  • Unknown: The extent to which his claimed trauma influenced his conduct, and any prior investigations into his online activity before the raid.

Practical implications

  • Publishing future works: Rights holders may reassess contracts; some retailers could choose to pull his titles pending further review.
  • Legal precedent: The case underscores Australian courts’ willingness to impose custodial sentences for possession and distribution of child exploitation material, even for high‑profile individuals.
  • Verification: Readers can confirm the sentencing details through the Western Australian District Court’s public register and view Silvey’s full apology on his Substack page (search “Craig Silvey My Apology”).

Reactions

  • Fans and literary peers expressed shock, dismay and disappointment on social media, echoing the sentiment Silvey described in his apology.
  • Victim‑advocacy groups warned that the circulation of such material re‑traumatizes survivors and called for robust enforcement of child‑protection laws.
